title: Image Classification Pipeline
summary: The end-to-end image classification pipeline, and why transfer learning is almost always the right start.

slides.subTitle: Preprocessing, CNN backbone, softmax output
slides.markdown: A standard pipeline has three stages. **Preprocessing**: resize to a fixed input size, normalize pixel values (typically to the mean/std the backbone was pretrained on), and optionally augment. **CNN backbone**: a stack of convolutional layers extracts progressively higher-level features — edges and textures in early layers, parts and shapes in middle layers, whole-object concepts in later layers — ending in a fixed-length feature vector, usually via global average pooling. **Classification head**: a small fully-connected layer maps that feature vector to class logits, and **softmax** converts logits to a probability distribution over classes. The backbone is where almost all the representational power lives; the head is often just one or two layers.

slides.subTitle: Crop, flip, color jitter
slides.markdown: Augmentation applies random, label-preserving transformations to training images — random crops, horizontal flips, rotation, color jitter (brightness/contrast/saturation shifts) — creating effectively more training variety from the same labeled set. It matters **more** here than in most other ML domains because image datasets are expensive to label and models are large relative to typical dataset size, so overfitting risk is high; augmentation is a nearly free way to reduce it. A caveat: augmentations must actually preserve the label — flipping a digit "6" horizontally can turn it into something resembling a "9", so augmentation choices need to match what's actually invariant for the task, not applied blindly.

slides.subTitle: Fine-tuning an ImageNet-pretrained backbone
slides.markdown: Instead of training a CNN from random weights, take a backbone already trained on a huge, general dataset (ImageNet, ~1.2M images, 1000 classes) and adapt it to your task. The early and middle layers of an ImageNet-trained CNN already encode generally-useful visual features (edges, textures, shapes) that transfer across almost any vision task — you're not starting from zero, you're starting from a model that already "knows how to see". Typically you replace the final classification layer with one matching your class count, then fine-tune some or all of the network on your (often much smaller) labeled dataset. This is why transfer learning is the default starting point for nearly every practical image classification project.

slides.sectionTitle: Training from scratch vs transfer learning
slides.subTitle: The data/compute trade-off
slides.markdown:
| | From scratch | Transfer learning |
|---|---|---|
| Data needed | Large (tens of thousands+ labeled images per class) | Small (can work with hundreds per class) |
| Training time/compute | High — days on multiple GPUs for a strong result | Low — hours on a single GPU |
| Risk of overfitting on small data | High | Low, since most weights are already well-generalized |
| When it makes sense | Your domain is very unlike natural images (e.g. satellite radar, medical scans with unusual modalities) | Nearly always, for standard photographic images |

How to decide: default to transfer learning; only train from scratch when you have both a genuinely large labeled dataset and a domain visually unlike what ImageNet-style backbones were pretrained on.

slides.subTitle: ResNet, EfficientNet, and how to choose
slides.markdown: **ResNet** (2015) introduced residual/skip connections that let very deep CNNs (50, 101, 152 layers) train without vanishing gradients — it remains a strong, simple, well-understood default. **EfficientNet** systematically scales depth, width, and input resolution together (compound scaling) to get better accuracy per unit of compute — a good choice when inference cost or model size is tightly constrained (mobile, edge deployment). In practice: reach for a mid-size ResNet as a fast, reliable baseline; move to EfficientNet (or a Vision Transformer, covered under [Vision Beyond CNNs](vision-beyond-cnns)) when you need to squeeze out more accuracy per FLOP or need a smaller deployable model.

slides.subTitle: Fine-tuning too aggressively destroys pretrained features
slides.markdown: A common beginner mistake: fine-tuning a pretrained backbone with the same learning rate you'd use to train from scratch. Pretrained weights already encode useful, carefully-learned features — a large learning rate causes large gradient updates that can wreck those features in the first few steps, effectively throwing away the pretraining benefit before the model has learned anything new. The fix: use a **much smaller learning rate** for fine-tuning (often 10–100x smaller), and/or freeze early layers entirely for the first few epochs, only unfreezing and fine-tuning the whole network once the new classification head has stabilized (a technique sometimes called "discriminative fine-tuning" or gradual unfreezing).

slides.subTitle: Two ways to reuse a pretrained backbone
slides.markdown:
There are two distinct ways to reuse a pretrained backbone, not one. **Feature extraction** freezes the entire backbone and only trains the new classification head — fast, needs very little data, and works well when your images are visually similar to the pretraining domain. **Full fine-tuning** unfreezes some or all backbone layers and updates them too, at a low learning rate — slower and needs more data, but adapts the features themselves when your domain differs meaningfully from natural photos.

A practical default: start with feature extraction to get a quick baseline, then fine-tune the last few backbone blocks if accuracy plateaus below what the task needs.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: how little data transfer learning needs
slides.markdown:
A from-scratch CNN on a 20-class problem with 200 labeled images per class will typically underfit badly — that's roughly 4,000 total images spread across 1000x more parameters than the data can constrain. The same 20-class problem, starting from an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 with only the head retrained (or the last block fine-tuned), can often reach 85-90%+ top-1 accuracy on that same 4,000-image set.

The gap isn't a training trick — it's that the pretrained backbone already spent its "data budget" learning general edge/texture/shape features on 1.2M images, so your small dataset only has to teach it the last, task-specific step.

**Wrong belief:** "My classifier hits 95% accuracy, so it's working well."

**Why it's wrong:** if one class makes up 95% of the training and test data (a common real-world skew — most manufacturing defect or medical screening datasets are dominated by the "normal" class), a model that always predicts that one class also scores 95% accuracy while catching zero of the cases that actually matter.

**Correct model:** check per-class precision/recall (or a confusion matrix) whenever classes are imbalanced, not just overall accuracy — a rare-class recall of 0% is invisible in the aggregate number but is usually the whole point of the system.
